newsitem.title: UK: Strong U.S. oil consumption brakes oil price fall.
newsitem.headline: Strong U.S. oil consumption brakes oil price fall.

text.p: The United States' thirst for crude oil has halted a dramatic drop in oil prices this year, but with inventories on the rise and Iraq close to resuming exports the reprieve will be brief, an energy watchdog group said Tuesday.
The Paris-based International Energy Agency revised upward its forecast of 1997 world oil consumption by 100,000 barrels a day to 73.8 million due mainly to strong growth in U.S. oil consumption.

"Demand growth (in the second quarter) appears to have been very robust, led by strong U.S. gasoline demand and continued high growth rates in several Asian and Latin American developing countries," the IEA said in its monthly report.
Crude oil prices are about $19.65 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange, down from $25 last year.

But provided that Iraq starts exporting oil as expected under the terms of a U.N. oil-for-food accord and supply from outside the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries continues to grow, prices will come under further pressure as storage tanks fill up.

"Projections of world demand and non-OPEC supply for the remainder of the year suggest that there will be very substantial increases in inventories, unless OPEC crude oil output is reduced significantly," the IEA said.

World oil inventories are estimated to have risen by 1.6 million barrels a day in the second quarter, leaving stocks in the leading industrial economies 74 million barrels higher than at the end of June last year.
For the rest of this year, demand growth and increases in non-OPEC supply of 2 million barrels daily are expected to cancel each other out, displacing even more OPEC barrels into storage.

"Even if the high final product demand growth rates seen during the last two months are extended through the next two quarters, crude production will outstrip demand by an average 1 million barrels a day in 1997, with most of the (stock) build taking place in the second part of the year," said the Washington-based Petroleum Finance Co.
"While demand growth is expected to remain strong, its impact on oil prices may be offset by rising stock levels," it said.
The absence of Iraqi exports in June cut OPEC output by 580,000 barrels to 26.4 million, still well above the IEA's estimate of average 1997 demand for the cartel's barrels of 25.7 million.
Once Iraqi production returns to normal later this month or early August, the pace of the stock building will increase and could push world oil prices into a new lower range, analysts said.
"The return of Iraqi crude to the export markets is the most important near-term wild card for world oil supply," the IEA said.
Baghdad suspended exports of around 660,000 barrels in late May after reaching the $2 billion cash limit for the first 180 days of the U.N. accord.
The deal was renewed on June 8 but Iraqi authorities, unhappy with a cumbersome process for distributing aid, have delayed the resumption of exports.
The U.N. hopes to receive the revised Iraqi food distribution plan by Tuesday, clearing the way for Iraq to start shipping oil again within a few weeks, industry sources said.
